query: For high-entropy-alloy multilayer protective coatings, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain their resistance to time-dependent plastic deformation? Specify what governs the behavior and why, an unspecified controlled comparison that would reveal it, the expected observations relative to a baseline, applicable boundaries, supporting evidence, and an outcome that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In high-entropy alloy multilayer protective coatings, reducing the individual layer thickness below a critical value (≈10 nm) increases the density of amorphous-like interfaces, which in turn delocalizes strain by shifting the deformation mode from concentrated shear banding to a more distributed kinking-like mechanism. This change suppresses time-dependent plastic deformation under sustained loading.
generation.material_initial_state: Multilayer protective coatings based on high-entropy alloys with well-defined individual layers that, at larger thicknesses, tend to form discrete shear bands under load.
generation.intervention: Fabricate and compare coatings with varying individual layer thicknesses (e.g., 10 nm versus 40 nm), keeping the overall alloy composition and processing conditions constant.
generation.conditions: Conduct time-dependent mechanical tests such as nanoindentation creep or sustained bending under controlled moderate stress and temperature conditions that simulate service environments.
generation.structural_mediator: The high density of amorphous/amorphous interfaces resulting from ultrathin (≈10 nm) layers.
generation.mechanism: In thinner layers, the increased interface density interrupts the formation of localized shear bands, promoting a transition to a kinking-like deformation mode that spreads out strain across multiple layers. This strain delocalization improves resistance to creep and other time-dependent plastic deformations.
generation.predicted_outcome: Coatings with ~10 nm thick layers will exhibit lower creep strain, more uniform deformation (reduced shear band concentration), and sustained hardness over time compared to thicker-layered coatings (e.g., 40 nm), which are expected to show conventional shear band-dominated plastic deformation.
generation.baseline: High-entropy alloy coatings with thicker individual layers (~40 nm) that display clear, localized shear banding under sustained loading and greater time-dependent plastic deformation.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies when the alloy retains an amorphous or near-amorphous interfacial structure and is tested under moderate stresses and temperatures. It may not hold if the material crystallizes or in extreme loading/thermal environments.
generation.uncertainty: The exact critical layer thickness and the universality of the mechanism may vary with alloy composition and processing history. The scalability of these effects to industrial conditions also warrants further investigation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare high-entropy alloy multilayer coatings with controlled individual layer thicknesses (e.g., 10 nm and 40 nm). Subject both sets of samples to identical time-dependent loading tests (e.g., nanoindentation creep or three-point bending under constant load) and analyze the deformation mechanisms using high-resolution microscopy to visualize the presence or absence of localized shear bands.
measurements: Microstructural characterization of deformation zones (e.g., shear band density and morphology)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the coatings with ~10 nm layers do not show significantly reduced creep strain or if they exhibit similar localized shear banding (i.e., no transition to kinking-like deformation) compared to the thicker (~40 nm) coatings under identical conditions, then the hypothesis would be deemed falsified.

## Abstract
AbstractExtensive research has shown that nanolayered structures are capable of suppressing the shear banding in metallic glass in nanoindentation experiments. However, the specific mode and mechanism of the shear banding underneath the indenter remains unknown. Also, the quantification of shear banding-induced strain localization is still a challenge. Herein, the size-dependent shear banding behavior of a CuTiZrNb high-entropy alloy-based nanolayered glass with individual layer thicknesses (h) ranging from 5 to 80 nm was systematically investigated by nanoindentation tests. It was found that the hardness of the designed structure was almost size-independent. Yet, a clear transition in the deformation modes from the cutting-like shear bands to the kinking-like ones was discovered as h decreased to 10 nm. Moreover, multiple secondary shear bands also appeared, in addition to the primary ones, in the sample with h = 10 nm. The transition leads to an obvious strain delocalization, as clearly illustrated by the proposed theoretical model, which is based on the assumption of a pure shear stress state to quantify the shear banding-induced strain localization.
